scenes.title: Multi-Region DNS: global zones, regional paths
scenes.narration: This architecture is about one DNS namespace with independently managed regional network infrastructure. Begin at the purple private hosted zone in the center, which contains application and database records and is associated with VPCs in Regions A and B. The zone can serve both VPCs, but the large blue and orange regional boxes are deliberately separate. In Region A, identify the local VPC Resolver, inbound endpoint network interfaces, outbound endpoints, and Resolver rules. Region B has its own equivalent infrastructure, and neither Region inherits the other's endpoints automatically. Now follow the orange arrows down to corporate DNS forwarders. Each corporate environment targets deliberate inbound endpoint IP addresses over suitable hybrid connectivity; resilient choices across Availability Zones matter. Notice the five callouts along the bottom. The hosted-zone scope is not the same as a regional Route 53 Resolver Profile or endpoint. Create regional networking and DNS rules where needed, choose forwarder targets deliberately, then separately confirm that returned application IPs are reachable. Test endpoint, AZ and Region failures, plus client caches. The takeaway is to share the name where appropriate, while planning and operating each regional DNS path as its own failure domain.

scenes.title: DNSSEC: sign the zone, validate the answer
scenes.narration: The slide separates DNSSEC signing from DNSSEC validation. On the left, Route 53 signs a public hosted zone. Its key-signing key, or KSK, signs the DNSKEY record set, while the zone-signing key, or ZSK, signs the zone's record sets. Follow the arrow to the parent zone's DS record. That delegation signer record links the parent trust chain to the hosted zone's public key, provided the parent is configured correctly. Now turn to the cyan panel. A VPC client asks the VPC Resolver for a signed public DNS name, and DNSSEC validation, when enabled, checks cryptographic signatures and the chain of trust. Valid authenticated answers can be returned; a broken signing chain, incorrect DS or invalid signature may lead to SERVFAIL. The lower cards emphasize the operational boundary: Route 53 hosted-zone signing applies to public zones, not private hosted zones. DNSSEC protects answer authenticity and integrity, but it does not encrypt DNS queries and does not replace TLS for application traffic. An unsigned insecure delegation is not automatically a DNSSEC error. Plan key rollover, monitor signer health, and troubleshoot signing and validating settings separately.

scenes.title: Diagnose DNS results before changing the network
scenes.narration: This is a DNS troubleshooting decision framework. Start with the four large columns and read the returned status before changing any route or security group. A timeout means no timely answer, so examine which DNS server was queried, the path to it, port fifty three and endpoint health. NXDOMAIN means the requested name was not found; confirm spelling, selected hosted zone, VPC associations, forwarding rules and negative caching. NODATA means the name exists but lacks the requested record type, for example a AAAA lookup without a matching record. SERVFAIL means the resolver failed to complete resolution, potentially because of upstream reachability, DNSSEC validation, forwarding loops or applicable firewall behavior. Then follow the six cards along the bottom in order: identify caller configuration, capture the exact name and record type, establish which resolver answered and its status, determine the effective zone or forwarding rule, inspect logs and caches, then retest consistently. The green final note is crucial. NOERROR with an answer means DNS worked for that query, but TLS, networking or the application might still fail. Treat each status as evidence, not as a single guaranteed root cause.

scenes.title: Scenario: resilient hybrid DNS across accounts
scenes.narration: This scenario combines the DNS concepts into a multi-account, two-Region architecture. On the left, corporate DNS remains authoritative for corp dot example dot com, while users need to resolve AWS private names. The center network account manages an AWS private zone such as aws dot example dot com, along with supported shared DNS rules or Profiles for workload accounts. Three workload accounts consume appropriate associations rather than each inventing a different DNS design. Now look at Region one and Region two. Both have inbound and outbound Resolver endpoint capacity across two Availability Zones. Corporate DNS conditionally forwards the AWS-owned suffix toward AWS inbound endpoints, while AWS Resolver forwards the corporate-owned suffix through regional outbound endpoints to corporate DNS targets. These directions must not form a forwarding loop. The bottom four solution panels call for the right hosted-zone sharing, carefully associated forwarding rules, private VPN or Direct Connect routing, port fifty three security and observability. Query logging and DNS Firewall can add controls, but cached answers and Region or endpoint loss still need active tests. The final caution separates successful DNS resolution from successful application connectivity. Estimate endpoint and query-processing costs while validating both directions from real client views.
